Interview with Lawrence Brown
by Patricia Willard
Reel Six

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395

Interview with Lawrence Brown. This is July 3rd, 1976. Lawrence, I was reading in Max Jones' and John Chilton's book on Louis Armstrong that the band at the Cotton Club was led by a trumpet player named Vernon Elkins until Les Hite took over. Tell me a little bit about the band then.

Well, the band was smaller than Les Hite's band, and Elkins was -- well, he was not the musician that Les Hite was, and so therefore it wasn't up to par, we would say, and the greatest thing about the band at that time was when Louie, in 1930, came out as a solo artist and naturally he fronted the band, and from then on, why it was a different band in that the arrangements were better and the solos were more interesting and it was just a better organization, until Les Hite came.
And then he was a better musician, or more used to arranging and framing up the bands. He sang and he was more of a leader. That's when the band became very nice, we'd call it.
You were saying that the solos became better, the arrangements became better, after Louie arrived. You mean he inspired everyone to play better music?
Well, he gave them a different understanding of what they were playing. Before he came they were
just playing the pieces, but when he came he inspired them to think in a different vein on their solos and work so that it was more interesting. He brought life to the organization.
Who was doing the Overwriting arrangements?
Well, they were more just the general -- fellows were just framing things themselves, but well, the whole group had a different atmosphere in their thinking, so it was better than before.
